h1: Setting up a brewery in India as a foreign company
title: Setting Up a Brewery in India | Craft Beer School
desc: The routes a foreign company can take to brew in India: own plant, joint venture, acquisition or contract brewing plus the steps each one involves.
teaser: There are four ways in. Each trades control against speed and cash.
standfirst: A foreign company can brew in India through its own plant, a partner, a purchase or someone else's equipment. This guide compares the routes and lists the steps that apply to all of them.
sections: Four routes to brewing in India

The first route is a wholly owned plant. You buy land, build, equip and license a brewery yourself. It gives the most control and takes the most time and cash.

The second is a joint venture with an Indian partner. The partner may bring land, licences, distribution or local knowledge. You bring brand, technology and skill. The agreement between you decides how well it works.

The third is buying an existing brewery or a stake in one. It shortens the wait for licences but brings the history of the business with it, so due diligence matters.

The fourth is contract brewing at a host plant, which lets you sell before you build. Our guide on contract brewing in India for international brands covers it in detail.
Why India is not one market

Alcohol is a state subject in India. Each state sets its own licences, excise duty, pricing rules, brand registration and rules on how beer reaches the shop or bar. These rules differ between states and they change.

Several states, including Bihar and Gujarat, have prohibition. Others restrict sales in various ways. For a brewery this means the choice of state is a business decision. Our guide on choosing an Indian state goes through the factors.
Steps that apply to every route

• Decide the structure: a company in India, a branch or a partnership. Take advice from a lawyer and a chartered accountant who know foreign investment rules
  • Choose the state and then the site, with a licensing adviser who works in that state
  • Obtain the manufacturing licence, premises approvals and registrations that state requires
  • Register the brand and labels with the state excise authority where required. Protect the trademark too
  • Arrange water, power, effluent treatment and pollution control approvals
  • Plan raw material supply, including malt and hops, which may be imported
  • Build the distribution route the state allows

None of this is quick. The order varies by state. Do not buy equipment before you know the site can be licensed.

Technical planning is the part you probably know. Fit it to Indian conditions. Heat adds load to refrigeration. Water quality varies by location and may need treatment. Power supply can be less steady than you expect, so check backup arrangements. Cold chain to the customer is often the weak link for beer.

Choose the size from a realistic demand plan, not from the brand's global scale. A project report tests the idea on paper before money is spent. See our guide on expanding or buying contract capacity for the economics of building against renting.

Staff need brewing skill, plus someone who understands excise paperwork and state-level compliance.
What to expect on time and cost

We do not quote durations or costs here because they depend on the state, the site and the plant. Build your timeline from what your licensing adviser and engineers tell you. Add contingency for approvals. Delays in licences are common.

Plan the cash for the quiet months before the first sale. Our guide to how breweries are valued helps if you intend to buy rather than build.

We support companies from abroad that want to brew in India. That includes comparing routes, outlining the licensing process with your state adviser, planning the plant and the team and setting up quality and costing systems. The work runs remotely by video call and shared data, with site visits by arrangement.

We are not a law firm and not a licensing agency. You will need licensing advisers and lawyers for those steps. We work alongside them. We do not name clients or promise outcomes or timelines.
Questions to settle before you commit

Ask first what you want the Indian business to be. A showcase for a global brand needs a different plant from a volume producer for local supply. Ask who will manage it day to day and whether that person has run a licensed brewery.

Ask how you will get cash out. Rules on moving money across borders and on foreign ownership can change. Take advice from a chartered accountant and a lawyer before you fix the structure.

Finally ask what you will do if a licence is delayed by a year. A plan that survives that delay is a plan you can trust.
faqs: Can a foreign company own a brewery in India?
Rules on foreign investment apply and can change. Take advice from a lawyer and an accountant familiar with them before you decide on a structure.
Is contract brewing easier than building?
It is usually quicker and needs less cash. You depend on the host. State rules still apply to the arrangement.
Do I need a separate licence in each state?
Alcohol is a state subject, so licences and rules are set by each state. If you brew or sell in several states, expect to deal with each one.
